items.title: The Settlement Mill Is The Part Of Personal Injury Law Nobody Wants To Talk About
items.summary:
There is a term lawyers sometimes use when talking among themselves that you probably won’t find on a law firm’s website.

Settlement mill.

It’s not a particularly flattering description, and that’s the point. It generally refers to a personal injury practice that operates on volume. Bring in as many cases as possible, move them through a relatively standardized process, negotiate settlements, collect fees, and make room for the next group of clients.

Now, I want to be careful here because I think this subject deserves considerably more thought than it usually gets.

Settling personal injury cases is not a bad thing. Quite the opposite. Most cases settle, and many absolutely should. Litigation can be expensive, emotionally exhausting, and painfully slow. A fair settlement can put money into the hands of an injured person when it is needed most, without the uncertainty of asking a jury to decide what happens next.

I’ve recommended settlements throughout my career. I’ve also advised clients against accepting offers that, in my judgment, failed to account for what they had lost.

Both decisions are part of doing the job properly.

My concern is what happens when settling cases becomes less about professional judgment and more about keeping a business operation moving.

And I think we need to talk about that.

When the Business Gets Bigger Than the Case 

Personal injury law looks considerably different today than it did when I began practicing.

Advertising is everywhere. Television commercials, billboards, social media campaigns, sponsored search results, and increasingly…

items.title: Trump administration withdraws application to Supreme Court to block lower court ruling on protected status for Venezuelan nationals
items.summary:
Originally published on Nov. 18; updated with latest developments on Nov. 19 at 4:35 p.m. 

The battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon. Specifically, the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 ruling by a federal judge in San Francisco that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the court that if they do not act, the order by U.S. District Judge Edward Chen “will spring into effect, inflicting severe and immediate harm.”

Then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023. In 2025, he announced that the program would be extended through October 2026. Mayorkas cited a “severe humanitarian emergency” resulting from the “severe political and economic crisis” in Venezuela as the reason for the designation.

After Mayorkas’ successor, Kristi Noem, announced her decisions to end Venezuela’s designation and its subsequent extension, a group representing TPS holders went to federal court in San Francisco to challenge those decisions. Chen set them aside, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit upheld that ruling. In 2025, while that litigation was moving forward, the Supreme Court paused Chen’s order with regard to Venezuela, effectively clearing the way for the Trump administration to deport Venezuelan TPS beneficiaries while the case continued.

items.t: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to block lower court ruling keeping protected status in place for Venezuelan nationals

items.title: Kirkland’s $125 Million Trump Deal Was Never Written Down, But The Hours Sure Were
items.summary:
Ever since Kirkland & Ellis signed up for its $125 million pro bono payola deal in April 2025, the world’s richest law firm has had one answer to everyone who asked what it actually promised Donald Trump: a politely worded shrug. Now, a year and a half and six congressional letters later, we finally have numbers.

Quick refresher for anyone who blocked out early 2025: weeks into his second term, Trump started issuing executive orders against Biglaw firms he decided had crossed him. Those orders told agency heads to strip lawyers’ security clearances, restrict personnel from accessing federal buildings, and slash federal contracts held by the firms’ clients. The four firms that sued — Perkins Coie, Jenner & Block, WilmerHale, and Susman Godfrey — are doing victory laps in court. But nine other firms took a different route. Paul, Weiss went first , and Trump rescinded the order against Paul, Weiss after it agreed to provide $40 million in pro bono work for conservatice causes. Then came Skadden , Willkie , Milbank , and Cadwalader , then Kirkland, Latham, Simpson Thacher, and A&O Shearman . The final tally was $940 million collectively in pro bono help toward causes supported by Trump, the war chest we’ve been calling pro bono payola ever since.

New reports from the New York Times and MS NOW are both based on a seven-page letter Kirkland sent to congressional Democrats on November 5, signed by the firm’s outside counsel, Beth Wilkinson. As of Oct. 28, Kirkland had logged about 6,491 hours of free work for the Trump administration, valued at $11.8 million. The Commerce…

items.title: Handling The Holidays As A Young Lawyer
items.summary:
Your family wants to know when you are coming home. The partner wants to know when the draft will be ready. Your friends want you at dinner. Your bank account would prefer that you stay home. Somewhere in the middle, someone tells you to enjoy the most wonderful time of the year. You would settle for knowing whether you can leave the office on Wednesday.

The holidays can be difficult when you are learning how to practice law. You have responsibilities you cannot ignore and expectations you do not yet know how to manage. You may feel guilty at work because you want to leave and guilty at home because you brought work with you. After nearly 30 years of practice, my advice is to make specific plans, communicate them early, and allow yourself a holiday that fits your circumstances.

Find Out What Actually Needs to Be Done 

Uncertainty can consume your entire holiday. A partner says, “Let’s get this done before the end of the year,” and you hear, “Cancel your flight.” Before you rearrange your life, ask what the assignment requires and when the partner needs it. Does the draft need to go to the client Friday? Does someone need time to review it? Could you deliver the important section before leaving and finish the rest afterward? You cannot plan around an expectation you have invented.

Review your matters before the office starts emptying. Look beyond the days you will be away to the first week back. Identify what needs attention, who will handle it, and what information that person needs. Ask your supervising lawyer to confirm priorities when assignments compete. A short…

items.title: Attacking Judge Over Free Speech Only To Run Face First Into Sanctions Is Perfect Metaphor For LSU Football
items.summary:
Every child ordered to apologize for smacking their sibling has pulled the “you can’t make me” retort. And they’re technically correct. But they soon learn that parents can absolutely take away their toys when they don’t hear an apology.

Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill is on the cusp of learning the same lesson.

Back in September, the SEC sued LSU in federal court in Alabama because Lane Kiffin tried to sign former NFL players to play for the team with the blessing of a friendly state judge. LSU backed down, but the case kept going anyway — because now LSU wants to add a former basketball professional — and in an October 20 reply brief, Murrill told the court that “key SEC citations … appear to be negligently supplied or hallucinated .”

On Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Annemarie Carney Axon had some thoughts about that accusation given that the cases were absolutely real . LSU’s local counsel, Bruce Rogers, conceded the cases were real — “They’re not made-up cases” — and argued “hallucinated” was a broader term for LSU just not agreeing with the citations.

This strategy worked… poorly .

Axon asked Rogers, “Do you consider attacks on people’s professional reputation and character to be legitimate advocacy?”

Rogers said no.

“You wouldn’t want somebody to wrongly accuse you of hallucinating a case, knowing full well what the implication of that accusation is,” Axon said.

Rogers again said there was a broader definition to the term “hallucinated.”

“We’re not dressing this up, OK?” Axon said. “You put the pig out there. There’s no time for you to put lipstick…
items.t: Attacking Judge Over Free Speech Only To Run Face First Into Sanctions Is Perfect Metaphor For LSU Football

items.title: Calls for court packing fail the test of history
items.summary:
Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff. 

***

As Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify. One especially prominent proposal has been to expand the court to 13 justices. In the last few months, we have seen former Vice President Kamala Harris say the Supreme Court should be increased to this number. In August, Rep. James Clyburn, a longtime Democratic leader in the House, endorsed this proposal on “Meet the Press.” Just in the past few weeks, Hillary Clinton said the party “should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power.” Potential presidential candidate Pete Buttigieg has advocated increasing the number of justices to 13 as well.

Some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications. Take Hillary Clinton’s proposal, for instance. “It used to be that you’d have one justice for each circuit,” Clinton explained. “We now have 13 circuits, we should have 13 justices.” Buttigieg has also argued for modifying the size of the court on that basis. But the symmetry argument is pretextual: It is no mere coincidence that the reintroduction of a one-to-one justice to circuit relationship under Democratic control would produce exactly the four seats needed to transform the current six-to-three conservative majority into a seven-to-six liberal one. Such a proposal then allows advocates to cover their desire for change to the court’s size in the language of a seemingly neutral…
items.t: Calls for court packing fail the test of history

Time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket . Under the Supreme Court’s typical briefing schedule , a case must be granted by mid-January to be briefed in time for the final argument session, which begins this term on April 19.

But despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review . Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers, state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms, and the regulation of prediction markets like Kalshi.

Understanding the timeline 

Before we explore some of the major issues pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket. (For more on this process, read law professor Stephen Wermiel’s SCOTUSblog column from last week.)

Litigants file a petition for review, also known as a petition for certiorari, at the Supreme Court when they want the justices to review a lower court ruling against them. In their petition, they lay out, among other things, their views on why the ruling was wrong and why the issue is worthy of the justices’ attention.

After a petition is filed, the litigants that prevailed before the lower court (known as the respondents) have 30 days to respond, although they may ask for additional time. Sometimes, they file a brief in which they agree that the Supreme Court should take up the issue, but it’s far more common for…
items.t: Five major issues that may still make it onto this term’s oral argument docket

items.title: Work-Life Integration For Lawyers Who Want Their Time Back
items.summary:
When I started my coaching business in 2004, I had networking meetings in the morning, more of them at night, and a desk covered in business cards from people I was supposed to follow up with. Most weekends were already spoken for by family commitments. Today, I rarely work nights or weekends, and I can take a morning or an afternoon off without feeling like the whole business will come to a screeching halt. If you’d told me back then that I could have that kind of flexibility, I would’ve asked what the hell you were talking about. Today I’d call it work-life integration.

So, what is work-life integration for lawyers? Where work-life balance can sound like giving work and home equal time every day, work-life integration is about making those commitments fit together over the course of a real week. You might put in a late night before a filing and still be able to take Friday afternoon off. The trouble starts when every night turns into a late night and Friday afternoon is the first thing you give up. The real challenge here is in finding efficiencies that allow you to achieve your goals without adding to your already jam-packed schedule. 

Here are three changes that helped me get some control back and that I now work on with lawyers.

Become A Student Of Time Management 

When I started my business, I had stacks of paper on my desk, stacks of business cards from people I needed to follow up with and enough unopened emails that finding the one I actually needed felt like a project. At one point, my assistant and I gathered all the loose paperwork into a single pile. It…

items.title: Can You Legally Ditch Work And Family Chores To Play ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ In Peace?
items.summary:
In less than 24 hours, “Grand Theft Auto VI” will be available to play. As one of the most anticipated games ever, there is speculation that its release will negatively affect workplace productivity and divert spending away from other forms of entertainment, including bars and amusement parks.

Rockstar in its infinite wisdom opted to release the game at midnight local time on a work night. Most people will either wait until the next day to play or play the game for a few minutes after midnight before going to bed.

But the true GTA fans will grab their espresso, Red Bull, or their energy drink of choice and play until they crash out at 4 a.m. While some had the foresight to request time off from their job, others did not and will have to choose between going to work half-asleep or not show up to work and explain why to their boss.

Most people will attempt to binge-play the game for hours or even days with no interruptions. To head off family discord, some fans have drafted tongue-in-cheek “leave me alone” contracts. For a set period, the player is exempt from chores and relatives agree to refrain from interruptions or snide remarks.

For employees wanting time off to play the game, planning could help a lot.

Only a few states require giving employees paid time off (PTO) or paid vacation. Employers generally offer PTOs as a fringe benefit. Since PTOs can be used for any reason, including playing a video game, an employee does not have to disclose why he or she is using it. But in most cases, an employee must give their employer adequate notice and the employer must…

items.title: The Supreme Court before it stood apart
items.summary:
The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A. Shelden (The University of North Carolina Press)

***

In her excellent new book,  The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History , professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.

That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court. But Shelden’s history shows that the 19th century court and the way Americans perceived it were very different. Indeed, the modern idea of the detached judge, the justice as apolitical “ umpire ,” is not nearly as  originalist  as we tend to assume.

Shelden opens with Abraham Lincoln arguing before the court in 1849. The court that Lincoln and his fellow members of the bar knew was not the marble institution, removed from ordinary political life, that we picture today. For example, the justices “rode circuit.” Each was assigned a region, generally the part of the country from which he hailed and in which he traveled through to preside over federal trial courts. This brought the justices into regular contact with local lawyers, officials, and communities.

Shelden calls this “judicial representation”: the idea that a justice would bring a region’s perspective to the court because he knew the people he impliedly represented. Although today’s justices are assigned to a circuit, typically the circuit to which they have ties geographically, the concept is now decidedly different;…
items.t: The Supreme Court before it stood apart

items.title: Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once
items.summary:
On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing. This question now sits at the court in two pieces: a statutory question the justices have agreed to answer, and a constitutional one still waiting for the right case. Together, the answers will decide whether people who have lived here for years, even decades, can ask a judge to release them while they fight deportation.

***

Until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a) . According to this provision, ICE may release a detainee on bond subject to an immigration judge’s review (unless Section 1226(c)’s criminal- and terrorism-related provisions apply). In July 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement began requiring – for the first time – that anyone who had entered the United States without inspection, whether last year or decades ago, be detained instead under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) for the length of removal proceedings. Unlike Section 1226(a), this provision holds that immigration judges have no power to grant such detainees bond. Two months later, the Board of Immigration Appeals agreed with ICE in Matter of Yajure Hurtado .

Under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal…
items.t: Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

items.title: Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently
items.summary:
Two of the most enduring rights in the Constitution are the First Amendment’s protections of the free exercise of religion and the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause. Should the court’s approach to these rights vary? Specifically, should it be easier to prove discrimination under the free exercise clause than under equal protection?

At the oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy , on Nov. 3, several of the conservative justices in their questions suggested that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down. That is in sharp contrast with a half century of law under equal protection holding that disparate impact (seemingly neutral policies that result in negative effects on a particular group) is not enough to prove discrimination. I would not be surprised to see such “free exercise exceptionalism” from the Roberts court. But it seems to me unjustified.

St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy 

Colorado, in 2024, adopted a universal preschool program where it will provide funds for children to attend public, secular private, or faith-based preschools. The condition for receiving funds is that the school must consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.”

St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colorado, which has a Catholic preschool, and two parents brought a challenge arguing that this restriction on funding violates their free…

items.title: ‘Nothing they said made sense’: down the rabbit hole with Britain’s sovereign citizens
items.summary:
It is an anti-government ideology that began in the US and has spread across the world – wasting public resources and ruining lives. But why have the wild ideas of this movement become so appealing?

In the early morning of 20 June 2023, 13 police officers raided a five-bed barn conversion in rural Hampshire. The occupant, a 57-year-old man named Iain Clifford Stamp, was rudely awoken. The police informed him that they were executing a warrant on behalf of the Financial Conduct Authority, the body that regulates financial services in the UK. FCA raids are rare. They are only permitted when the regulator can persuade a judge that there are reasonable grounds for believing the person or firm that they are investigating will not cooperate. In this case, it seems, there was good reason to believe that Iain Clifford Stamp might cause trouble.

Stamp’s frosty relationship with financial authorities dated back to 2008, when his first company, a financial product provider called Integrity, imploded and was left facing claims from clients of up to an estimated £80m. Back then, Integrity had been publicly censured by the Financial Services Authority for not fairly communicating to customers the risks in the products it was selling. This time was more serious.…

items.title: Listening to the past
items.summary:
Originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is. That is because it holds that we should give the Constitution its original meaning, and the text of the Constitution does not always make that meaning readily apparent to modern readers.

In a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians. Maybe, I concluded , but they can still be good (originalist) judges.

A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge. Judges must be decisive, but historical inquiry is often inconclusive. This month’s column considers this criticism – specifically, two common forms that it takes: (1) originalism attributes too much significance to historical silence, and (2) originalism cannot reconcile dissonant historical traditions.

The role of history in text-and-history cases 

Originalists turn to the historical record for a variety of purposes. Because originalism holds that the Constitution means today what it meant in 1789 (except to the extent that it has been lawfully amended), understanding the meaning of its words requires looking to historical sources to figure out how those words were used at the time the Constitution was ratified. To take an uncontroversial example, while a modern reader might read “domestic violence” and think “spousal abuse,” historical context reveals that “domestic Violence” in the guarantee clause means internal civil unrest.

Sometimes, however, originalists look to the historical record for purposes other than uncovering the contemporary…
items.t: Listening to the past

items.title: “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket
items.summary:
Justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his new book, “ So Ordered .” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket. First, applications on it now rival the number of cases the court decides after full briefing and oral argument. Second, this growth can be traced to presidents who govern by executive order, which produces lower-court rulings that move quickly to the Supreme Court. Third, he does not expect the trend to reverse. “Unless something changes there, and I don’t foresee it right now,” he said, “I’m afraid this is going to continue.” Alito added, such “[a]n application is something that I think we have to rule on.”

Readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice. The 2025-26 term, which ended on Oct. 4, provides the receipts. And the data support part of what Alito said but complicate the rest.

The volume fell, but not to normal 

In the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court. In the 2025-26 term, it filed 12. Every other applicant held steady. States filed nine applications in the 2024-25 term and 8 last term, and private parties filed 19 and 20. The entire decline came from the executive branch.

For most of the past quarter century, the federal government rarely asked the court for such relief. It filed 6 applications across the 2000-01 through 2015-16 terms, never more than one in a single term. That changed during the first Trump…
items.t: “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket
